title: SHE STOPPED ASKING GOD FOR A SON—THEN THE PROPHET TOLD HER, “THIS TIME NEXT YEAR, YOU WILL HOLD HIM”
paragraphs: SHE STOPPED ASKING GOD FOR A SON—THEN THE PROPHET TOLD HER, “THIS TIME NEXT YEAR, YOU WILL HOLD HIM”
The Shunammite woman had learned how to live with an unanswered prayer. Then Elisha spoke one sentence that reopened the part of her heart she had apparently taught herself not to touch.
There is a kind of heartbreak that cries loudly.
And there is another kind that eventually stops crying.
That second kind may be harder to recognize.
You still get out of bed. You still welcome people. You still serve. You still worship. You still make room for others. You can laugh at the table and sincerely thank God for what you have.
But somewhere inside you is a room you rarely enter anymore.
Because once, you prayed there.
Once, you hoped there.
Once, you imagined something beautiful happening there.
And after enough years passed...
you quietly closed the door.
That is where we meet the Shunammite woman.
Her story is recorded in 2 Kings 4:8–37, and Scripture does not even give us her name.
It simply introduces her as a woman from Shunem.
Yet what happens inside her home becomes one of the most emotionally astonishing stories in the ministry of Elisha.
She was not introduced as desperate.
She was not begging the prophet for a miracle.
She was not chasing Elisha down the road asking him to give her a child.
In fact, that is precisely what makes her story so piercing.
She had apparently learned how to live without one.
Scripture describes her in Hebrew as:
אִשָּׁה גְדוֹלָה
ishah gedolah.
Literally, “a great woman,” an expression commonly understood in context as indicating a woman of standing or prominence.
She had resources.
She had a home.
She had influence.
She had a husband.
And she had enough discernment to recognize something sacred when Elisha repeatedly passed through Shunem.
She told her husband:
“Behold now, I perceive that this is a holy man of God, which passeth by us continually.”
—2 Kings 4:9, KJV
Then she did something beautiful.
She made room.
She asked her husband to prepare a small chamber for Elisha, furnished with a bed, a table, a stool, and a candlestick.
Nothing spectacular.
No stage.
No applause.
No promise that her generosity would purchase a miracle.
She simply honored the man of God because she recognized that he belonged to God.
That distinction matters.
This passage must never be twisted into a transaction.
The Shunammite woman did not buy a miracle with hospitality.
God is not a vending machine, and generosity is not a lever by which human beings force heaven to give them what they want.
Grace cannot be purchased.
But her hospitality revealed something about her heart.
She made room for the things of God without demanding that God fill the empty room inside her.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You still serve God...
but there is something you stopped asking Him for.
You still pray for everybody else.
You encourage people whose prayers seem to be answered faster than yours.
You celebrate pregnancies while carrying private infertility.
You attend weddings while wondering whether companionship will ever come.
You congratulate someone on the opportunity you secretly wanted.

You tell people God is faithful while standing in front of a grave, a diagnosis, a broken relationship, a financial disaster, an addicted child, a prodigal son or daughter, or a future that looks nothing like the one you imagined.
You believe in God.
You just don't know whether you can survive hoping for that particular thing again.
One day Elisha wanted to honor this woman for the kindness she had shown him.
Through his servant Gehazi, he asked what could be done for her.
Could Elisha speak to the king?
Could he speak to the commander of the army?
Her response is striking:
“I dwell among mine own people.”
She wasn't looking for status.
She wasn't asking for political influence.
She wasn't trying to turn proximity to the prophet into personal advancement.
Then Gehazi noticed what the woman herself had not requested.
“She has no son, and her husband is old.”
There it was.
The sentence behind the silence.
No son.
An aging husband.
Humanly speaking, the window was closing.
Elisha called her.
She stood in the doorway.
And then the prophet touched the wound she had not volunteered.
In Hebrew, 2 Kings 4:16 reads:
לַמּוֹעֵד הַזֶּה כָּעֵת חַיָּה אַתְּ חֹבֶקֶת בֵּן
La-mo'ed hazzeh ka'et chayyah, att choveqet ben.
The sense is:
“At this appointed time, about this time next year, you shall embrace a son.”
Not merely see him.
Not merely hear about him.
Embrace him.
חֹבֶקֶת — choveqet.
Holding.
Embracing.
Imagine what those words did to her.
Perhaps everyone else would expect excitement.
Instead, something almost painful comes out of her mouth.
She answers:
אַל אֲדֹנִי אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים אַל תְּכַזֵּב בְּשִׁפְחָתֶךָ
Al, adoni, ish ha'Elohim; al tekhazzev be-shifkhatekha.
“No, my lord, thou man of God, do not lie unto thine handmaid.”
In other words:
Please don't do this to me.
Please don't awaken something I have already buried.
Please don't make me hope again if I am going to be disappointed again.
That may be one of the most human responses to a miracle promise anywhere in Scripture.
Because sometimes disappointment does not destroy faith in God.
It destroys your willingness to expect.
There is a difference.
You can believe God is good while being terrified to believe something good could happen to you.
You can believe God performs miracles while quietly assuming your name isn't on the list.
You can believe Jesus heals while trembling every time the doctor's phone number appears on your screen.
You can believe God restores marriages while yours is falling apart.
You can believe God saves prodigals while wondering why your child seems farther from Christ than ever.
You can believe in resurrection...
and still weep beside the tomb.
The Bible makes room for that kind of trembling.
The woman conceived.
And according to the word spoken through Elisha, she gave birth to a son.
Imagine that first cry.
Imagine the tiny fingers.
Imagine the first time she held against her chest the child she had been afraid even to hope for.
The prophecy had become warm flesh in her arms.
The impossible had a heartbeat.
But if the story ended there, it would be beautiful.
Scripture doesn't end it there.
Years pass.
The boy grows.
One day he goes out to his father among the reapers.
Suddenly he cries:
“My head, my head.”
He is carried back to his mother.
And 2 Kings 4:20 gives us one of the most devastating sentences in the chapter:
“He sat on her knees till noon, and then died.”
Read that slowly.
The child she had never asked Elisha to promise...
the child she had been afraid to hope for...
the child God had given her...
died in her arms.
Now the story becomes frighteningly familiar.
Because some people reading this did receive what they prayed for.
And then lost it.
You got the relationship.
Then it collapsed.
You got the job.
Then the company let you go.
You finally became pregnant.
Then came the devastating appointment.
Your loved one recovered.
Then the illness returned.
Your child came back to church.
Then disappeared again.
You thought the nightmare was over.
Then your phone rang.
There is a particular agony in losing something after you finally allowed yourself to believe it was safe to love.
The Shunammite woman carried her dead son upstairs.
And where did she place him?
On the bed of the man of God.
The room she had once built for ministry became the room where she laid her impossible situation.
Then she shut the door.
She went to find Elisha.
Her husband apparently did not yet understand what had happened.
When Gehazi saw her approaching and asked whether everything was well with her, her response was:
שָׁלוֹם
shalom.
“It is well.”
Do not misunderstand her.
The boy was still dead.
Biblical faith is not pretending tragedy isn't real.
Faith is not calling death life.
Faith is not smiling while secretly bleeding because Christians are supposedly forbidden to grieve.
The Psalms destroy that idea.
Jesus Himself wept.
Her shalom did not mean nothing was wrong.
Her subsequent actions show how deeply distressed she actually was.
When she reached Elisha, she caught hold of his feet.
Gehazi moved to push her away.
Elisha stopped him.
“Let her alone; for her soul is vexed within her.”
Her soul was bitter.
Then the words finally came out:
“Did I desire a son of my lord? did I not say, Do not deceive me?”
There it is.
The wound underneath the miracle.
I didn't ask you to awaken this hope.
I didn't ask you to give me something I would love this much.
Why give it to me if this is how the story ends?
Maybe you have never spoken those words aloud.
But God has heard their echo inside you.
Why did You let me meet them?
Why did You open that door?
Why did You let us become pregnant?
Why did You restore it only to let it break again?
Why did You allow me to believe?
Why, God?
Scripture does not shame her for asking.
Elisha goes to the house.
He enters the room.
The child lies dead on his bed.
Elisha shuts the door.
He prays to the LORD.
Then the text describes an unusual, intensely physical scene. Elisha stretches himself upon the child, mouth upon mouth, eyes upon eyes, hands upon hands.
The child's flesh becomes warm.
Elisha walks back and forth through the house.
Then he returns and stretches himself upon the boy again.
Suddenly...
the child sneezes seven times.
And opens his eyes.
Elisha calls Gehazi.
“Call this Shunammite.”
She enters.
And Elisha says:
שְׂאִי בְנֵךְ
Se'i venekh.
“Take up thy son.”
Four words in English.
But imagine being that mother.
She had carried his dead body into that room.
Now she would carry him out alive.
She falls at Elisha's feet.
Bows to the ground.
Then takes her son.
And leaves.
But there is something we must be very careful about here.
This passage does not promise that every Christian who loses a child will receive that child physically back in this present life.
It does not promise that every infertile couple will conceive within a year.
It does not teach that enough faith guarantees the miracle we request.
And it would be cruel to weaponize this story against grieving people by suggesting that an unanswered prayer proves deficient faith.
This is a historical account of God's extraordinary work through His prophet Elisha.
Yet it points beyond Elisha.
Because Elisha could enter a room and pray for resurrection.
Jesus Christ entered our world as the Resurrection and the Life.
Elisha called upon the LORD.
Jesus could stand before a tomb and command:
“Lazarus, come forth.”
Elisha was God's prophet.
Jesus is God's Son.
And this is where the Shunammite woman's story reaches beyond one miraculous afternoon in Shunem.
Because our deepest problem is greater than infertility.
Greater than disappointment.
Greater even than physical death.
Our deepest problem is sin.
Scripture says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
—Romans 3:23
And:
“The wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
—Romans 6:23
We were not merely disappointed people needing encouragement.
We were sinners needing reconciliation with God.
Spiritually helpless.
Unable to purchase redemption.
Unable to perform enough good deeds to erase our guilt.
Unable to resurrect ourselves.
Then Jesus came.
The sinless Son of God lived the righteousness we could not live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day...
the grave did not get the final sentence.
Jesus rose.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Not that Christians always get the ending they wanted in this life.
But that everyone who belongs to Christ has a hope death itself cannot ultimately destroy.
The Shunammite woman received her son back temporarily in this mortal life.
But eventually both mother and son would still face physical death.
Jesus offers something infinitely greater.
Resurrection life that death cannot reclaim.
Forgiveness that your past cannot cancel.
Grace that your scandal cannot outrun.
A new identity that your worst chapter cannot name.
That is why the Gospel is not self-improvement.
It is resurrection.
Maybe your dead place is not a child.
Maybe it is your faith.
Maybe somewhere between unanswered prayers, betrayal, church hurt, secret sin, addiction, pornography, shame, grief, divorce, rejection, disappointment, or years of pretending...
something inside you stopped expecting God to meet you there.
You still know Christian language.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know the songs.
You know the verses.
But privately?
You are exhausted.
And perhaps the most dangerous sentence you have whispered is not “I don't believe in God.”
It is:
“I don't want to hope anymore.”
Listen carefully.
God does not owe us the particular miracle we have imagined.
Christianity does not guarantee an easy life.
Jesus explicitly taught His disciples that they would experience trouble.
But the Gospel gives us something stronger than the guarantee that circumstances will obey our wishes.
It gives us Christ Himself.
And if you have Christ, your story is not ultimately being written toward a grave.
It is being written toward resurrection.
There may be things God restores here.
There may be things He asks you to surrender.
There may be prayers answered dramatically.
There may be prayers whose answers you will not understand this side of eternity.
There may even be graves you must walk away from without seeing them open today.
But for the person united to Jesus Christ, the grave is never the final chapter.
Paul writes that if we believe Jesus died and rose again, God will bring with Him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus.
Christian hope does not deny death.
It announces death's expiration date.
And perhaps that is why this unnamed woman still speaks thousands of years later.
She teaches us that faith can tremble.
Faith can ask painful questions.
Faith can fall at God's feet without having polished words.
Faith can carry the unbearable into the room.
And grace can meet us there.
Maybe your prayer tonight doesn't need to sound impressive.
Maybe it needs to sound like:
Jesus, I am tired.
Jesus, I am angry.
Jesus, I don't understand.
Jesus, I have sinned.
Jesus, I have been hiding.
Jesus, I am afraid to hope again.
Jesus, forgive me.
Jesus, save me.
Jesus, I surrender.
Because the greatest miracle isn't getting everything you once dreamed about.
The greatest miracle is a sinner being reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
If you have been running from Him, come home.
Repentance is not God demanding that you clean yourself before approaching Jesus.
Repentance is turning from sin and turning toward the Savior who alone can save you.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the dead dream.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the thing you hope nobody discovers.
The cross already proves Jesus knows exactly what sin costs.
And the empty tomb proves sin and death do not get the final word.
That is what we mean when we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing consequences with religious slogans.
But by forgiving sinners, making them new, redeeming what evil meant for destruction, and transforming people who could never transform themselves.
If this story exposed a room inside your heart you have kept locked for years, don't rush away from that conviction.
Be honest before God.
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need evidence that another believer has walked through darkness without abandoning Jesus.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God. It doesn't.
Not because sharing Christian content makes anyone more righteous. Only Christ can make us righteous before God.
Someone has stopped hoping.
Someone is grieving.
Someone's marriage is collapsing behind smiling photographs.
Someone is ashamed of what they did last night.
Someone believes God could forgive almost anybody except them.
Someone may never search for a sermon.
Send this to the mother who needs encouragement.
Send it to the father who has stopped talking about what hurts.
Send it to the believer who feels spiritually numb.
Send it even to the friend who isn't sure they believe any of this anymore.
Because there may come a night when you need to read it again.
Supporting Gospel work does not purchase God's blessing, salvation, answered prayer, or spiritual status. Those things cannot be bought.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God with the resources He has entrusted to you, supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one expression of generosity and partnership—alongside your local church, care for people in need, missions, personal discipleship, and other biblically faithful giving.
Jesus remains the message.
Jesus remains the Savior.
Jesus remains the One we want you to remember.
So comment if you need prayer.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is sitting beside something they thought God would never allow to die.
And perhaps they don't need somebody promising that God will give them exactly what they want.
Perhaps they need someone reminding them that Jesus Christ walked into death Himself...
and walked back out.
When you belong to Jesus, even the chapter that looks like a grave does not have permission to call itself the ending.
